title: Electronic trap monitoring systems reduce operator response time during live trapping for harvest in Germany
content:
by Franziska Sommer, Kathrin Büttner, Johannes Lang, Michael Lierz

Live trapping of mammals is practiced worldwide for purposes including pest control, wildlife harvest, species conservation, and research, with increasing emphasis on animal welfare. Electronic trap monitoring systems (ETMS) aim to reduce confinement time of captured animals by enabling faster trap checks. We conducted a field study to evaluate whether commercially available ETMS reduce operator response time and work reliably under practical trapping conditions. Between 2022 and 2024, volunteer trappers from Germany tested 91 devices from 4 commercial ETMS. During the first phase, trappers could not access the ETMS notifications (simulating non-electronically monitored traps), whereas in the second phase they received notifications. We also included data from experienced trappers operating privately owned ETMS. Response time was defined as the time between trap trigger and check. We evaluated ETMS reliability based on user-friendliness, malfunctions, and server-related issues. Median response time decreased significantly from 8.06 h in the non-notified group (n = 118) to 6.05 h in the notified group (n = 132), corresponding to a reduction of 2.01 h (25%) when using ETMS. Experienced notified users (n = 268) showed a median response time of 6.08 h. Retired trappers had significantly shorter response times when ETMS were used (4.43 h, n = 59) than employed trappers (7.36 h, n = 73). Installation errors, malfunctions, and server-related issues caused notification failures in 2 ETMS, whereas the other 2 operated reliably. Reduced response time can improve animal welfare, as prolonged confinement increases the risk of stress and injury. We strongly recommend ETMS where sufficient mobile network coverage is available. Minimum technical standards for ETMS should be defined and verified by independent institutions.
